questions: What sets the sign of ΔH - the height of the hump or where the products sit?
Where does the activation energy appear on this profile?
segments.say: Exothermic: products lie below reactants. Draw the reactants level, climb the activation-energy hump, then fall to the products: the enthalpy change is negative and heat leaves the system. Keep your student notes open at the enthalpy change definition for this scene.

questions: How is this profile different from the exothermic one, in one sentence?
Does an endothermic reaction still have an activation energy?
segments.say: Endothermic: products lie above reactants. The reaction absorbs heat, ΔH is positive, and it still clears an activation-energy barrier. Compare the two profiles side by side in your student notes before we move from energy to speed.

questions: Which curve is the faster reaction, and what did you read to decide?
Name two changes that would make the gentle curve steeper.
segments.say: Rate curves: steeper means faster. Rate is the fall in reactant concentration over time, and the gradient of the curve is the rate. Raise the temperature or add a catalyst and the curve steepens. Now try the rate reading on the worksheet in pairs.

questions: What happens to the activation energy itself when the temperature rises?
Why does a small temperature rise make such a big difference to the rate?
segments.say: Maxwell–Boltzmann: more molecules past Ea at higher T. Most molecules sit near the average energy and only the fast tail can react; heating flattens and shifts the distribution so that tail grows. Check the Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution definition in your student notes, then look ahead to the exit ticket question on this scene.

questions: Adding nitrogen made more ammonia - which principle predicts that?
If the temperature alone changes Kc, what must happen to Kc when only the pressure changes?
segments.say: Le Chatelier: the system opposes the change. Add nitrogen and the Haber mixture makes more ammonia; compress it and it shifts toward fewer gas moles. Kc itself only changes with temperature. Work the Kc calculation on the worksheet now, in pairs.

questions: In one sentence, what does a catalyst actually change about an equilibrium?
How would you correct a classmate who insists a catalyst must mean more product at equilibrium?
segments.say: A common mistake: a catalyst shifts equilibrium. The animation grows both rate arrows by the same factor and the equilibrium bars never move: equilibrium arrives sooner, in the same place, with the same Kc. Finish the worksheet trap question now, then the exit ticket on your own - the first question revisits exactly this scene.
segments.watchFor: A catalyst pushes the equilibrium toward the products. Listen and look for it on the worksheet and in pair talk: any answer giving the catalyst a shifted equilibrium shows the trap reading, not the rates reading - send them back to the two equally grown arrows in this scene and to the correct turn: A catalyst speeds the forward and reverse reactions equally: the position of equilibrium is unchanged.
